records.name_note: Admissible sources split on the name. NC State's dedicated page for this exact taxon renders the H1 'Crocus tommasinianus', and its Common Name(s) list holds a single entry, 'Woodland crocus' (the same name also appears in the page's <title> metadata), but its description calls the plant 'Snow Crocus'. RHS's dedicated page for this exact taxon leads with 'early crocus'. 'Tommies' does not appear on either fetched page. Woodland crocus was chosen as primary because it is the first and only entry in NC State's Common Name(s) list.
records.toxicity_detail: No cat- or dog-scoped toxicity statement was found on an admissible page for this species. RHS's species page carries a "Potentially harmful" block reading "Ornamental bulbs - not to be eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." and a Pets line reading "Ornamental bulbs - not to be eaten - see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants for further information and useful contact numbers". That pets line names no animal and gives no symptoms, poison part list or severity rating, so it does not support toxic_to_pets. NC State's page for this species carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats/Dogs tags. Toxicity was not borrowed from Colchicum autumnale or other crocus species.
unknowns: Missouri Botanical Garden / plantfinder.mobot.org could not be fetched (connection refused for non-browser clients), and Clemson HGIC returned 403, so neither contributed evidence. No dedicated Clemson, UF/IFAS, PSU, UMD or UGA page for this exact species was read.

toxic_to_pets left null: the only admissible toxicity text (RHS) says ornamental bulbs are 'not to be eaten' and names no animal. is_edible is set false on that RHS 'not to be eaten' statement; no source describes edible use.

soil_drainage left null: NC State says 'Plant them 3 to 4 inches deep and 3 to 4 inches apart in average well-drained soils.' and 'They prefer sandy soils and do not do well in poorly drained clay soil.', and RHS's Moisture field reads 'Well–drained'. That is a bare well-drained reading with no wet-tolerance statement, so no token was chosen. NC State's Soil Texture lists Sand only, while RHS's Soil Types read 'Chalk, Clay, Loam, Sand'.
soil_ph left null: RHS says pH acid or alkaline or neutral, so no ceiling or floor is supportable; NC State gives no pH.

mature_spread_in_min and mature_spread_in_max left null: NC State's Width value reads 'Width: 0 ft. 4 in. - 6 ft. 0 in.', which looks like a feet/inches transposition of a 4-6 in figure and is not usable, and RHS gives Max Spread '0-0.1 metre' (up to 3.9 in). Height uses NC State's species Dimensions value 'Height: 0 ft. 4 in. - 0 ft. 6 in.' (4-6 in); RHS's Max Height 'Up to 10 cm' (3.9 in) is slightly lower.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only. NC State's structured Light field lists 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', but its prose says 'They perform best in full sun but tolerate partial shade.' RHS's structured Position field lists Full sun only, and its description says 'Great for naturalising amongst dwarf grasses and tolerant of shade, so performs well in woodland areas too.' Partial shade is a tolerance in both sources and is excluded by RHS's Position field, so part_shade is not landed; light shade such as a woodland edge is tolerated.
water_regime left null: no watering statement on any fetched page for this species.

Temperature, humidity, light in foot-candles, fertilizer and chill-damage figures: no admissible-source statement found. RHS hardiness H6 and NC State zones 3-8 are survival ratings, not damage onset temperatures.

is_houseplant is false: no admissible source addresses indoor culture; NC State lists Landscape Location Lawn, Walkways and Woodland and USDA zones 3a-8b, and RHS treats it as a hardy (H6) outdoor bulb.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State's page for Trachycarpus fortunei carries no Poison block and no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag. Its Tags block reads: "#specimen #winter interest #salt tolerant #palm #evergreen #fantz #children's garden #tropical feel #non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #container plant #showy fruits #cycad #winter garden #wind tolerant #drought tolerant #year-round interest #broadleaf evergreen #clay soils tolerant #playground plant #frost tender #cpp #HS304 #HS111". The page has no handling warning and does not address eating the plant. RHS's page for this species says nothing on toxicity.
unknowns: Only two admissible pages could be read for this species: NC State and RHS. The Missouri Botanical Garden page (plantfinder.mobot.org, taxonid 276718) failed with a TLS certificate-verification error in the fetch tooling. The dedicated UF/IFAS page (ST645, Trachycarpus fortunei: Windmill Palm) returned HTTP 410 Gone. The Clemson HGIC windmill-palm page returned 403. The UF/IFAS EP020 page covers many palms and was not used. No claim here rests on any of these three.

Pet safety rests only on NC State's tags 'non-toxic for cats' and 'non-toxic for dogs'. NC State has no Poison block for this species. No other admissible source addressed toxicity. The same tag list also contains '#cycad', which does not describe this palm. Nothing was borrowed from sago palm or from palms in general.
is_edible is null. No admissible source addresses eating this palm. NC State only says leaf fibres are used for weaving and that the plant is used to make rope, brooms, mat, and cloth in China.

is_houseplant is false: NC State lists Landscape Location Container, Patio, Recreational Play Area and Walkways and USDA zones 7a-11b, and says only 'It can be grown in large containers and overwintered indoors in colder climates.'; RHS says it can also be grown as a conservatory or warm glasshouse specimen. Both are conditional statements, not a houseplant recommendation.

chill_damage_f is null. NC State gives USDA zones 7a-11b, a '#frost tender' tag and the prose 'it may suffer in the coldest locations'. RHS gives hardiness H5 with UK ratings. None of these is a damage-onset temperature.

Mature size uses NC State's Dimensions block (height 8 ft-10 ft = 96-120 in; width 4 ft-6 ft = 48-72 in). It is a cultivated size. NC State's prose says the palm reaches 20 to 40 feet tall in the wild and typically tops out around 10 feet in cultivation. RHS gives Max Height 'Higher than 12 metres', which is open-ended, and Max Spread 1.5-2.5 metres (59.1-98.4 in) over 20-50 years. RHS's figures are larger than NC State's, so the 96-120 in height range understates the species' potential size.

soil_drainage is moderate from NC State's pair Good Drainage plus Moist. RHS's moisture field says only 'Well–drained', which is ambiguous on its own and does not conflict. NC State's problems prose also mentions 'root rot'.
soil_base is null. NC State lists Container, Patio and other landscape locations, and RHS says 'well-drained' soil in the ground. Neither maps cleanly to one enum token.
soil_ph is null. NC State lists Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0) and Alkaline (>8.0), and RHS says 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral'. Together these set no floor or ceiling.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun and part_shade. NC State's Light field lists full sun and partial shade (2-6 hours of direct sun), and RHS Position lists Full sun, Partial shade. RHS's cultivation sentence on 'lightly dappled shade' was not used because it may be shared genus text.

water_regime is null. Neither page gives a watering instruction. NC State's Moist soil tag and Drought resistance tag and RHS's 'Drought Resistance Yes' are soil and tolerance traits, not watering statements. This is an in-ground palm, so dry-down target and day intervals are also null.

humidity, temperature ranges, light in foot-candles, direct-sun hours, fertilizer, pH bounds and pollinator attraction are not stated by NC State or RHS for this species. NC State has no Attracts field.

NC State's page for this binomial lists Trachycarpus wagnerianus under 'Previously known as' and also lists 'Wagnerianus' as a cultivar with smaller, stiffer leaves. records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox, dedicated page for Allium sphaerocephalon. The poison fields (Poison Severity, Poison Symptoms, Poison Toxic Principle, Causes Contact Dermatitis, Poison Part) come from NC State's Poisonous to Humans section, which is human-scoped; the page has no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag and names neither cats nor dogs (its Edibility caveat refers generically to "the person or animal"), so nothing here is a cat or dog finding. Page lead: 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.' Poison Severity: Low. Poison Symptoms: 'Poisonous if ingested. Symptoms may include nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. (Poison parts: All parts; bulbs, bulblets, flowers, and stems).' Poison Toxic Principle: Sulfides. Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part field lists: Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems. Co-listed tags and traits on the same page: Plant Type: Bulb, Cool Season Vegetable, Poisonous; Problems: Poisonous to Humans, Weedy; Resistance To Challenges: Deer, Drought; page tags include #poisonous and #edible. Edibility field (same page): 'Flowers, stems bulbs are edible. However, the plant also has poisonous characteristics as noted in the "Poisonous to Humans" section of this record.' It adds: 'Toxicity can depend on the age of the person or animal, the age of the plant, the part of the plant ingested, how much is ingested, whether the person or animal has sensitivities or allergies, whether it's eaten raw or cooked, and so forth.' and advises consulting a medical professional; no preparation times or conditions are given. No handling warning is stated. The page says the plant has an onion/garlic type aroma, and its Wildlife Value reads 'Deer and rabbit resistive'.
unknowns: Only NC State was reachable. The RHS page id for Allium sphaerocephalon could not be found (guessed slug 404, search is script-rendered) and MoBot (www.missouribotanicalgarden.org, plantfinder.mobot.org) failed to connect; Clemson HGIC returned 403 for a guessed URL and no UF/IFAS page was identified. records.name_note: Sources split on which common name leads. NC State's Common Name(s) list carries two entries in alphabetical order, Winter-flowered Jasmine then Winter Jasmine (its page-title parenthetical has the same order), but its own description prose calls the plant "Winter jasmine". RHS's page shows "winter jasmine" as the common-name subtitle under the H1 Jasminum nudiflorum and lists "winter-flowered jasmine" under Other common names. "Winter Jasmine" was chosen because RHS leads with it and NC State's prose uses it.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Plant Toolbox page for Jasminum nudiflorum carries these tags in one contiguous run: "#non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #pruning tolerant #pet friendly #playground plant"; its full tag list also includes #children's garden, alongside #deciduous, #shrub, #deer resistant and #black fruits. The page has no Poison block, no poison-part list, no symptom list and no handling warning. The tags are the only pet-safety evidence found. No toxicity was carried over from Gelsemium sempervirens or any other genus. RHS (the only other admissible page read) says nothing about toxicity.
unknowns: The Missouri Botanical Garden page for this species (kempercode=a152, which redirects to plantfinder.mobot.org) could not be fetched in this session. It failed with ConnectError and ProxyError, and curl hit a certificate error on the redirect. No MoBot content was used or cited. No dedicated Clemson or UF/IFAS page was located for this exact name, so only NC State and RHS were read.

is_houseplant is false: neither admissible page frames Jasminum nudiflorum as a houseplant. RHS lists it as a hardy outdoor deciduous shrub and NC State as a landscape plant (Landscape Location Coastal, Naturalized Area, Recreational Play Area, Rock Wall, Slope/Bank; USDA zones 6a-10b).

Mature size conflict. RHS gives Max Height 1.5-2.5 metres and Max Spread 1.5-2.5 metres (59.1-98.4 in, converted at x39.37), reaching maturity in 5-10 years. NC State's prose says 'Winter jasmine grows up to 4 feet tall. If it is grown as a vine, it will reach 10 to 15 feet tall and 3 to 6 feet wide', and its Dimensions block (Height 10 ft - 15 ft, Width 3 ft - 6 ft) matches the vine figures. Those are support or trellis dimensions, so they were not used. The RHS figures were used for all four size fields. NC State's 4 ft shrub figure (48 in) is lower than the RHS range.

outdoor_sun_exposure: NC State's structured Light field lists Full sun and Partial Shade, and RHS Position lists Full sun, Partial shade. NC State's prose says it 'will grow in heavy shade, but the floral display will be reduced'. That is a tolerance aside, so full_shade was left out.

soil_drainage is moderate from NC State's bare Soil Drainage pair 'Good Drainage' plus 'Moist'. RHS Moisture says only 'Well–drained'. NC State prose says it prefers well-drained soils but is adaptable and does well in poor soils.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poison block is human-scoped: its Problems field reads 'Poisonous to Humans', with Poison Severity 'Low' (the page lead says 'This plant has low severity poison characteristics.'). Poison Symptoms: poisonous through ingestion and dermatitis; sap causes skin and eye irritation. 'TOXIC ONLY IF LARGE QUANTITIES EATEN; SKIN IRRITATION MINOR OR LASTING ONLY FOR A FEW MINUTES.' Symptoms may include fever, swollen lips, thirst, nausea, diarrhea; skin irritation upon contact with cell sap. Poison Toxic Principle: Unknown. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part (full list): Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems. Co-listed tags: Plant Type values are Herbaceous Perennial, Houseplant, Perennial, Poisonous, Shrub, Vine; page tag #poisonous. NC State also notes the stems contain milky sap, and that leaves and roots are used as a laxative and emetic in traditional medicine, 'but large doses are toxic.' NC State carries no Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag for this species. RHS's page for this exact species states: 'Harmful if eaten; skin and eye irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling', and 'Pets (dogs, cats): Harmful if eaten; skin and eye irritant'. Handling: wear gloves and protective equipment (RHS); sap irritates skin and eyes (NC State).

records.name_note: Both dedicated pages lead with Burning Love. RHS's page title and its rendered subtitle under the H1 Ixora coccinea read burning love. NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized, its order matches the page-title parenthetical, and it begins with Burning Love. NC State's description prose opens with 'The jungle geranium', and NC State and RHS both list jungle geranium; RHS lists it under Other common names. UF/IFAS EDIS FP291 gives only 'Ixora'. NC State also lists the former name Pavetta coccinea. This is not a Pelargonium or Geranium: NC State places it in the coffee family (Rubiaceae).
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Plant Toolbox page has no Poison block. Its tag list includes "non-toxic for cats", "non-toxic for horses" and "non-toxic for dogs". The full tag list reads: shrub, moist soil, well-drained soil, red flowers, non-toxic for cats, non-toxic for horses, non-toxic for dogs, full sun tolerant, acidic soils tolerant, loamy soils tolerant, shrub border, background planting, bird friendly, black fruits, bonsai, broadleaf evergreen, butterfly friendly, container plant, foundation planting, hedge, low maintenance, purple fruits, screen, tropical evergreen, winter interest, slow growing. The UF/IFAS EDIS page says nothing on toxicity. NC State's Edibility field says "The ripened fruits are edible." That statement covers ripened fruit only and must not be read as covering leaves, flowers, stems or roots. NC State also notes that in India the flowers, leaves, roots and stems are used in traditional and folk medicine, which is not an edibility statement.

The RHS page for Ixora coccinea carries the name, Other common names, Family Rubiaceae, Native to GB/Ireland No and Name Status Correct. Its Size section reads only Time to Maturity No preference, and it has no cultivation, sun, soil, pH, toxicity or hardiness fields, so none were used.

is_houseplant is false: NC State says only that the shrub may be grown in containers and brought indoors in winter in colder climates, which is a conditional aside; NC State (USDA zones 9a-11b) and EDIS (hedges, borders, screens, specimen planting) describe it as a landscape shrub.
Edibility is conditional. Only 'the ripened fruits are edible' is stated (NC State). No source addresses the leaves, flowers, stems or roots as food.
toxic_to_pets=false rests on NC State's 'non-toxic for cats' and 'non-toxic for dogs' tags. NC State has no Poison block with symptoms or poison parts, and EDIS is silent.

Chlorosis in alkaline soil: NC State says 'Alkaline soils may cause chlorosis.' EDIS says foliage turns yellow in alkaline soil and that a micronutrient fertility program is needed. NC State's Soil pH is 'Acid (<6.0)', an open-ended band, so soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null.

chill_damage_f 50 comes from NC State's 'intolerant of temperatures below 50 degrees Fahrenheit'. NC State also says the shrub dies back in freezing temperatures, and gives zones 9-11. EDIS gives zones 10-11.

outdoor_sun_exposure is full_sun only. NC State's structured Light field is Full sun, and its prose says it 'can tolerate small amounts of afternoon shade'. EDIS's structured Light requirement reads 'plant grows in part shade/part sun', while its prose says 'Ixora thrives in full sun ... but can tolerate some shade.' part_sun and part_shade are left out: they rest only on the EDIS field, NC State's structured Light field excludes them, and both sources' prose frames shade as a tolerance.
Size sources differ. EDIS FP291 gives Height 10 to 15 feet and Spread 4 to 10 feet; NC State gives 4 to 6 feet by 3 to 5 feet. NC State was used as the anchor.

water_regime is null. The only moisture statements are the soil descriptors 'moist, well-drained'. There is no watering statement, and Ixora is an in-ground shrub, so the dry-down and interval fields are null.
Fertilizer interval and strength are not stated. EDIS says only that a continued micronutrient fertility program is needed in alkaline soil.
Humidity, temperature ranges, light in foot-candles and direct sun hours are not stated by admissible sources. NC State's '6 or more hours' is from a site-wide legend.
